Accessibility, workplace accommodation, and data representation determine whether AI expands or narrows participation.

Age effects are more visible through seniority. The post-LLM evidence points to greater exposure among younger workers in entry-level positions, while the cross-country pre-ChatGPT study finds no clear average age relationship in occupational exposure. These findings are not necessarily contradictory: exposure measured from occupation content differs from realized contraction in junior hiring.

### 5.4 Regions, countries, and development stages

National outcomes depend on occupational structure, human capital, digital infrastructure, industrial composition, firm capability, governance, and labor institutions.

The 23-country study finds average occupational AI exposure ranging from 0.52 in Lithuania to 0.72 in Finland. Differences across occupations are larger than differences across countries, but Northern European occupations are generally more exposed than Eastern European occupations. Within the same occupation, task content differs across countries, reflecting technology adoption and institutional organization.

The global 65-country study reports lower labor-force participation and higher productivity associated with AI development, while human capital and governance weaken the labor-displacing association. This suggests that adaptation capacity is not an afterthought; it is part of the mechanism connecting technology to employment.

Evidence from developing and transition economies remains incomplete but not irrelevant. Carbonero and colleagues develop task-based exposure measures for Lao PDR and urban Viet Nam. Lao PDR’s large agricultural workforce has lower mean suitability for machine learning and less task reorganization, while urban Viet Nam’s service and sales structure has higher exposure and greater potential for transformation. Gender differences are not statistically significant in their estimates, while younger Vietnamese workers face higher exposure than their Lao counterparts. The study shows why country-specific task content matters more than a simple ranking of technological maturity ([Carbonero et al.](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00191-023-00809-7)).

China demonstrates internal regional heterogeneity. Fang, Lin, and Liu find the largest wage effects in AI clusters and in Western provinces with developed complementary infrastructure. The provincial employment-structure study finds that AI’s effects vary across eight economic regions, with stronger high-skilled employment effects in technology-intensive coastal and industrializing areas. Spatial models indicate that AI development in one region can affect the employment structure of neighboring regions through industrial and economic spillovers ([Chinese provincial employment-structure study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10907740/)).

Like-for-like comparisons between advanced and emerging economies on AI-driven employment, wages, productivity, and job quality remain limited. Robot studies provide partial comparators, but robots are not interchangeable with software AI. A journal meta-review summarizes estimates in which industrial robots produced larger employment reductions in emerging economies than in developed economies, but those estimates concern robot adoption and cannot be directly generalized to generative AI ([AI labor-market meta-analysis](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00012-x)).

The principal risk for lower-income economies is not necessarily higher immediate exposure. It may be weaker capacity to generate complementary tasks, train workers, enforce labor standards, and retain value when AI adoption occurs through global production networks. At the same time, lower exposure can delay disruption and preserve employment in tasks that remain difficult to automate. The direction is therefore contingent, not predetermined.

### 5.5 Firms, institutions, and the distribution of gains

Large firms adopt AI earlier and can capture scale economies, data advantages, and productivity gains. Small firms may face capital, skills, and integration constraints, but they may also use accessible cloud and generative-AI tools without building large internal technology departments. The distribution of gains depends on which of these mechanisms dominates.

Governance affects both quantity and quality. Human capital and institutional quality moderate displacement in the global panel. Innovation systems condition the employment association in Europe: positive AI-exposure effects are concentrated in countries with stronger innovation capacity, while they are not evident in moderate or emerging innovators ([Guarascio and Reljic](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.econlet.2025.112183)).

Worker participation can also influence implementation. AI adoption that is co-designed, transparent, and accompanied by training is more likely to preserve discretion and trust. Adoption imposed through opaque monitoring and unilateral performance targets is more likely to produce insecurity and resistance. These institutional effects are difficult to estimate because worker voice is rarely measured consistently across countries and sectors.

## 6. Evidence Synthesis, Contradictions, Limitations, and Research Gaps

### 6.1 What the evidence supports most strongly

The evidence supports several conclusions with greater confidence than the headline question of whether AI creates or destroys jobs overall.

| Question | Best-supported judgment | Main qualification |
|---|---|---|
| Does AI restructure work? | Yes. Task content, skills, authority, and work organization change before aggregate employment necessarily changes | Exposure and adoption must be distinguished |
| Does AI displace labor? | Yes, in particular tasks, occupations, firms, and junior pathways | Evidence is not yet sufficient for a universal net-employment claim |
| Does AI augment labor? | Yes, especially in documentation, decision support, research, and hybrid professional work | Productivity gains can still be used to reduce headcount |
| Does AI raise productivity? | The literature is directionally positive | Most studies are observational and bundle AI with other digital technologies |
| Does AI increase wage inequality? | It can raise AI-skill premiums and within-firm disparities | Some groups, including women in selected Chinese service occupations, experience stronger wage gains |
| Does AI affect job quality? | Algorithmic control can reduce autonomy and increase insecurity and strain; augmentation can reduce burdens | Longitudinal and causal job-quality evidence is sparse |
| Are effects unequal across places? | Yes, through task structure, infrastructure, skills, institutions, and industrial composition | Comparable advanced–emerging-economy evidence is limited |

A recent thematic review of 2020–2025 research finds rising demand for technical and interdisciplinary skills, restructuring of work roles, wider wage differences between AI-skilled and non-AI-skilled workers, and extensive transformation rather than pure substitution. Its central conclusion is that organizational and institutional governance determines whether AI produces inclusive transformation or reinforces inequality ([The impact of AI on the labour market](https://doi.org/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y)).

The productivity review reaches a parallel conclusion from a different outcome. Positive productivity associations are common, but only four of 76 studies are experimental, and many combine AI with robotics, digital infrastructure, or broader transformation. This supports a productivity tendency, not a precise causal estimate.

### 6.2 Why the main findings appear contradictory

#### Net employment: displacement, neutrality, or expansion?

The employment disagreement arises because studies observe different margins.

The 65-country study measures labor-force participation and finds a negative association with AI development. The 23-country study measures employment growth by occupation and finds no clear average relationship, with positive associations in computer-intensive work. The UK study measures within-industry labor demand and finds negative effects without a significant employment-to-population result. The meta-analysis averages heterogeneous estimates and finds a near-zero pooled relationship. The Chinese firm study measures employment within listed manufacturers and finds expansion accompanied by role reallocation.

These results can coexist. AI may reduce participation for some workers, reduce demand in particular occupations, increase employment in complementary occupations, and leave national employment ratios statistically unchanged because the flows offset each other. Firm expansion can also increase employment for adopters while non-adopters lose market share or workers. A national employment measure may therefore conceal substantial redistribution.

The conclusion is not that one study is correct and the others are wrong. It is that “the effect of AI on employment” is not a single estimand. It must specify whether the outcome is participation, employment stocks, hiring, job postings, occupational demand, hours, firm employment, or the composition of jobs.

#### Industrial robots and AI exposure

Robots are more consistently associated with employment reductions than AI exposure. There are substantive reasons. Robot measures often capture operating capital stocks or installations, whereas AI measures frequently capture task exposure or job-posting language. Robots perform physical substitution in identifiable production settings; AI may augment a worker, enable another technology, or change tasks without requiring a new job title.

The European panel illustrates this distinction: robot density is negatively associated with employment growth, while AI exposure alone is not robustly associated and may partly offset robot losses. Treating robot evidence as direct evidence of generative AI would therefore exaggerate the certainty of AI displacement.

#### Wages: premiums, inequality, and heterogeneous gains

AI-skill premiums indicate scarcity and complementarity. Chinese firm evidence of higher employee and executive wages alongside greater pay disparities indicates that productivity gains may be distributed unevenly within firms. Robot evidence of no bottom-tail wage effect and a slight top-tail gain points toward distributional asymmetry. Chinese evidence of stronger female wage gains shows that not all distributional effects favor already advantaged workers.

The apparent contradiction disappears when wages are analyzed by skill, occupation, gender, firm role, and region rather than as one average. AI can raise wages for workers who complement it, reduce demand for substitutable tasks, and widen within-firm disparities at the same time.

#### Productivity and employment decoupling

Positive productivity and negative employment findings are not logically inconsistent. Productivity is output per unit of input; employment is the quantity of labor used. AI can raise output while reducing labor input. Whether total employment rises depends on output expansion, new products, complementary tasks, and labor mobility.

The global 65-country study explicitly frames this possibility as productivity–labor decoupling. The productivity review, however, shows that causal identification is weak in much of the literature. The key unresolved issue is whether AI-induced productivity gains expand demand enough to offset substitution in particular sectors and periods.

#### Augmentation and job quality

Healthcare evidence shows that AI can save time and increase capacity. Algorithmic-management evidence shows that a more efficient organization can also reduce autonomy and intensify work. This is not a contradiction in the data; it is a distinction between output and the conditions under which output is produced.

A system can reduce documentation time but increase visit targets. It can improve error response but reduce worker discretion. It can make scheduling more flexible while making income less predictable. Job quality must therefore be measured as a multidimensional outcome rather than inferred from productivity.

#### Bias and fairness

The LLM résumé study finds race- and gender-associated differences in model ratings, but the direction differs from conventional human callback patterns. This demonstrates that algorithmic bias is not necessarily a simple reproduction of human bias. It does not establish equitable hiring. The unresolved issue is how model evaluations translate into actual selection, how employers use them, and whether human oversight mitigates or amplifies them.

### 6.3 Methodological limitations

#### Exposure is not adoption

Potential exposure indices are useful for comparing task structures, but they do not show whether firms used AI. Job-posting measures capture stated labor demand, not actual hiring or employment. Firm-level adoption measures are closer to treatment, but adopters are selected and often differ from non-adopters in productivity, management, capital, and growth prospects.

This problem is especially severe for generative AI because adoption may be embedded in general software without a new job title or formal technology investment. A firm may train existing workers, outsource implementation, or integrate AI into a commercial platform. Neither AI vacancies nor patent counts will fully capture those changes.

#### Causal identification

The post-ChatGPT period overlaps with the pandemic recovery, inflation, interest-rate changes, technology-sector restructuring, and changing recruitment practices. A decline in postings may reflect AI, macroeconomic contraction, a shift from public postings to internal recruitment, or a combination.

Fixed effects and difference-in-differences designs improve identification, but they cannot automatically solve treatment timing, parallel-trend, or anticipation problems. The AI-scribe study uses a quasi-experimental design but remains observational and warns that adopters may differ from non-adopters. The Chinese wage and firm studies use fixed effects and other robustness procedures, but continuous AI demand remains endogenous to local growth and worker composition. The global panel studies cannot observe the firm-level mechanisms that generate country-level associations.

Randomized evidence is strongest for task performance, not employment. The physician trial randomizes access to an LLM and measures clinical performance; it does not randomize firms into AI adoption and observe employment. The gap between productivity experiments and labor-market outcomes remains substantial.

#### Employment measures lag behind task change

Job postings and platform tasks respond quickly. Employment stocks, wages, and labor-force participation adjust more slowly. A posting decline can precede layoffs, reflect lower recruitment for an expanding workforce, or represent the replacement of turnover rather than existing employment. Conversely, a firm may reduce hiring while retaining current workers, creating a labor-market effect that appears first in flows.

The short post-ChatGPT window also makes it difficult to distinguish transitional adjustment from permanent occupational decline. Historical automation often involved initial displacement followed by new tasks and reemployment, but the duration and distribution of that adjustment varied.

#### Sector and geography are difficult to compare

A percentage decline in job postings, a reduction in documentation minutes, a change in occupational switching, and a coefficient on labor-force participation are not interchangeable. Sectoral comparisons require common definitions of adoption, exposure, employment, productivity, and job quality. The literature rarely has them.

Geographic coverage is concentrated in Europe, North America, China, and other relatively data-rich settings. Algorithmic-management research is disproportionately concentrated in Europe, North America, and Asia, while Africa and Latin America account for a small share of empirical studies. Informal work, agricultural labor, small firms, and non-digital hiring channels are systematically underrepresented.

#### Job quality is weakly measured

The literature contains substantial conceptual and qualitative evidence on autonomy, surveillance, insecurity, and health, but fewer longitudinal measures. Cross-sectional surveys cannot establish causal ordering, and single-plant or single-platform cases cannot be generalized without comparative evidence. Even the AI-scribe study, which measures time use carefully, does not measure burnout or how saved time is distributed.

#### Reviews inherit the limits of their corpora

Systematic reviews improve synthesis but do not eliminate source heterogeneity. The productivity review excludes generative AI because high-quality empirical studies were limited at its search date. The post-LLM review includes working papers, reports, and other records in its eligibility framework, making its ranges useful for mapping an emerging field but unsuitable as a journal-only pooled estimate. Reviews of algorithmic management also vary in quality scoring, screening procedures, and the balance between conceptual and empirical sources.

### 6.4 Research gaps

The first priority is worker-level longitudinal evidence after ChatGPT. Studies should follow workers exposed to AI through displacement, reemployment, occupational switching, wage change, hours, mental health, and career progression. Employer posting data cannot answer these questions alone.

The second priority is linked firm–worker data. Researchers need measures of actual AI adoption, task assignment, individual productivity, training, employment decisions, and wage distribution within the same organization. Such data would help distinguish productivity augmentation from headcount reduction and identify whether new tasks are accessible to displaced workers.

The third priority is comparable sectoral measurement. Healthcare, finance, education, transport, creative work, software, manufacturing, and customer service need common outcome measures. The existing literature is strongest where work is digitally recorded and weakest where employment is informal, dispersed, or not advertised online. Direct field evidence for call-center work remains particularly underdeveloped.

The fourth priority is advanced–emerging-economy comparison. Research should measure not only exposure but also capacity to generate complementary tasks, provide training, regulate AI, and retain value within domestic economies. Africa, Latin America, South Asia, Southeast Asia, and informal work require substantially greater representation.

The fifth priority is distributional analysis. Race and ethnicity outcomes should be measured in actual hiring, promotion, wages, and dismissal rather than model ratings alone. Disability, gender, age, migration status, and their intersections also require worker-level evidence. The question is not merely who is exposed, but who has voice, training, mobility, and access to the gains.

The sixth priority is long-term job quality. Researchers need panel studies of autonomy, workload, monitoring, mental health, safety, job insecurity, and the quality of AI-adjacent work. Productivity gains should not be treated as evidence of improved work without measuring how control and responsibility are distributed.

The seventh priority is governance and worker participation. Comparative studies should examine whether collective bargaining, works councils, labor regulation, algorithmic transparency, appeal rights, and co-design alter employment and health outcomes. The evidence increasingly suggests that institutions are not external constraints on AI restructuring; they shape the technology’s practical form.

Finally, research must track more autonomous systems and agentic workflows emerging after 2025. These systems may alter the balance between assistance and substitution by completing multi-step tasks with less continuous human direction. Whether they produce a qualitatively different labor-market shock remains unresolved, and existing post-ChatGPT evidence is too short to answer it.

### 6.5 Closing judgment

AI is a major driver of the Fourth Industrial Revolution because it connects digital data and physical systems to adaptive prediction, generation, coordination, and decision-making. Its labor-market impact is therefore broader than the replacement of particular occupations. It changes the task content of jobs, the composition of firms and sectors, the value of skills, the organization of authority, and the distribution of risk.

The strongest evidence supports a conditional restructuring thesis. AI substitutes for some tasks, augments others, creates new complementary work, and shifts workers across occupational and organizational boundaries. Aggregate employment effects remain unsettled because displacement, production expansion, new-task creation, and institutional adjustment operate simultaneously. The practical and scholarly challenge is consequently not to choose between a universal displacement narrative and a universal augmentation narrative, but to identify the conditions under which AI’s productivity gains become secure, well-paid, and meaningful work rather than concentrated gains accompanied by weakened autonomy and unequal adjustment.
